claim: Sound analysis by the cochlea relies on frequency tuning of mechanosensory hair cells along a tonotopic axis.
source: Sound analysis by the cochlea relies on frequency tuning of mechanosensory hair cells along a tonotopic axis.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that represents established knowledge in auditory physiology.

claim: Tonotopy is associated with gradients of stiffness and resting mechanical tension in hair bundles.
source: We find that tonotopy is associated with gradients of stiffness and resting mechanical tension, with steeper gradients for outer hair cells, emphasizing the division of labor between the two hair-cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of stiffness and tension presented in the manuscript (Figures 2, 5).

claim: Outer hair cells show steeper gradients of stiffness and tension than inner hair cells.
source: We find that tonotopy is associated with gradients of stiffness and resting mechanical tension, with steeper gradients for outer hair cells, emphasizing the division of labor between the two hair-cell types.
evidence: This is directly supported by comparative data between inner and outer hair cells shown in Figures 2E and 5B-C.

claim: Tension in the tip links increases at reduced Ca2+.
source: We demonstrate that tension in the tip links that convey force to the mechano-electrical transduction channels increases at reduced Ca2+.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally through EDTA iontophoresis experiments shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: There are gradients in stiffness and tension at the level of a single tip link.
source: Finally, we reveal gradients in stiffness and tension at the level of a single tip link.
evidence: This is supported by calculations of single tip-link properties shown in Figures 3D and 5C.

claim: Mechanical gradients of the tip-link complex may help specify the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
source: We conclude that mechanical gradients of the tip-link complex may help specify the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and represents an inference about the functional role of the observed gradients.

claim: The cochlea is endowed with a few thousands of mechanosensory hair cells that are each tuned to detect a characteristic sound frequency.
source: The cochlea—the auditory organ of the inner ear—is endowed with a few thousands of mechanosensory hair cells that are each tuned to detect a characteristic sound frequency (Fettiplace and Kim, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Different frequencies are detected by different hair cells, which are spatially distributed in the organ according to a frequency or tonotopic map.
source: Different frequencies are detected by different cells, which are spatially distributed in the organ according to a frequency or tonotopic map (Lewis et al., 1982; Greenwood, 1990; Viberg and Canlon, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature on cochlear tonotopy.

claim: The hair bundle works as the mechanical antenna of the hair cell.
source: The hair bundle works as the mechanical antenna of the hair cell (Hudspeth, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Sound evokes hair-bundle deflections, which modulate the extension of elastic elements—the gating springs—connected to mechanosensitive ion channels.
source: Sound evokes hair-bundle deflections, which modulate the extension of elastic elements—the gating springs—connected to mechanosensitive ion channels.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of mechanotransduction in hair cells.

claim: Mechanical stress is conveyed to the mechano-electrical transduction channels by oblique proteinaceous tip links that interconnect the stereocilia near their tips.
source: Importantly, mechanical stress is conveyed to the mechano-electrical transduction channels by oblique proteinaceous tip links that interconnect the stereocilia near their tips (Pickles et al., 1984; Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on tip link structure and function.

claim: Electron microscopy and molecular dynamics simulations have suggested that the tip link may be too rigid and thus that a compliant element in series with the tip link could determine the gating-spring stiffness.
source: Electron microscopy (Kachar et al., 2000) and molecular dynamics simulations (Sotomayor et al., 2010) have suggested that the tip link may be too rigid and thus that a compliant element in series with the tip link could determine the gating-spring stiffness.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies using electron microscopy and molecular dynamics.

claim: The gating spring could reside within the assemblies of molecules that anchor both sides of the tip link to the actin core of the stereocilia.
source: If so (but see Bartsch et al., 2018), the gating spring could reside within the assemblies of molecules that anchor both sides of the tip link to the actin core of the stereocilia (Michalski and Petit, 2015), or perhaps be associated with membrane deformations at the lower insertion point of the tip link (Powers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Tip-link tension has been estimated at ~8 pN in the bullfrog's sacculus.
source: Tip-link tension has been estimated at ~8 pN in the bullfrog's sacculus (Jaramillo and Hudspeth, 1993) but, to our knowledge, there has been no such report in the mammalian cochlea.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific measurement in the bullfrog.

claim: There has been no report of tip-link tension in the mammalian cochlea prior to this study.
source: Tip-link tension has been estimated at ~8 pN in the bullfrog's sacculus (Jaramillo and Hudspeth, 1993) but, to our knowledge, there has been no such report in the mammalian cochlea.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of the study.

claim: Electrophysiological properties of the transduction apparatus vary with the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
source: Electrophysiological properties of the transduction apparatus, including the activation kinetics and the conductance of the transduction channels, as well as the kinetics of adaptation, have been shown to vary with the characteristic frequency of the hair cell (Ricci et al., 2003; Ricci et al., 2005; Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Beurg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The morphology of the hair bundle varies systematically with the characteristic frequency of the corresponding hair cell in vertebrate auditory organs.
source: In addition, it is a ubiquitous property of vertebrate auditory organs that the morphology of the hair bundle varies systematically with the characteristic frequency of the corresponding hair cell (Wright, 1984; Lim, 1986; Roth and Bruns, 1992; Tilney et al., 1992): going from the high-frequency to the low-frequency region of the organ, the hair bundle gets longer and comprises a progressively smaller number of stereocilia.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature on hair bundle morphology.

claim: Going from the high-frequency to the low-frequency region of the organ, the hair bundle gets longer and comprises a progressively smaller number of stereocilia.
source: In addition, it is a ubiquitous property of vertebrate auditory organs that the morphology of the hair bundle varies systematically with the characteristic frequency of the corresponding hair cell (Wright, 1984; Lim, 1986; Roth and Bruns, 1992; Tilney et al., 1992): going from the high-frequency to the low-frequency region of the organ, the hair bundle gets longer and comprises a progressively smaller number of stereocilia.
evidence: This describes the specific nature of morphological gradients supported by citations.

claim: Recordings were made at locations corresponding to characteristic frequencies of 1, 2, 4, and 15 kHz in the rat cochlea.
source: Recordings were made at locations marked by black disks, corresponding to characteristic frequencies (in kHz) increasing from the apex to the base of the cochlea as indicated on the figure and to fractional distances from the apex of 5%, 10%, 20%, and 50%.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Measurements were made from both inner and outer hair cells at the 1‒4 kHz locations.
source: We report measurements from both inner and outer hair cells at the 1‒4 kHz locations, but only from inner hair cells at the 15-kHz location.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection.

claim: Measurements were made only from inner hair cells at the 15-kHz location.
source: We report measurements from both inner and outer hair cells at the 1‒4 kHz locations, but only from inner hair cells at the 15-kHz location.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection.

claim: The rat cochlea was typically 10 mm long.
source: The rat cochlea was typically 10 mm long.
evidence: This is a measurement reported in the figure caption for Figure 1.

claim: Each hair bundle responded to a force step with a fast deflection in the direction of the stimulus followed by a slower movement in the same direction.
source: Each hair bundle responded to a force step with a fast deflection in the direction of the stimulus followed by a slower movement in the same direction (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Over the duration of the step, the deflection of the hair bundle increased in the direction of the applied step on average by 22% for inner hair cells and by 12% for outer hair cells.
source: Over the duration of the step, the deflection of the hair bundle increased in the direction of the applied step on average by 22% for inner hair cells and by 12% for outer hair cells, corresponding to an apparent softening of the hair bundle by the same amount.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: A mechanical creep is expected from mechanical relaxation of tip-link tension associated with myosin-based adaptation.
source: A mechanical creep is expected from mechanical relaxation of tip-link tension associated with myosin-based adaptation (Hudspeth, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed mechanical creep supported by a citation.

claim: The creep was strongly reduced upon tip-link disruption by EDTA treatment.
source: Accordingly, the creep was strongly reduced upon tip-link disruption by EDTA treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: For outer hair cells, a given series of force steps evoked hair-bundle deflections that decreased in magnitude towards more basal locations along the tonotopic axis.
source: For outer hair cells, we found that a given series of force steps evoked hair-bundle deflections that decreased in magnitude towards more basal locations along the tonotopic axis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The stiffness of outer hair-cell bundles increased with the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
source: Correspondingly, the slope of a bundle's force-displacement relation (Figure 2B), and thus stiffness, increased with the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
evidence: This is derived from the force-displacement data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The same behavior of increasing stiffness with characteristic frequency was observed for inner hair cells.
source: The same behavior was observed for inner hair cells (Figure 2C-D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: The stiffness gradient was steeper for outer hair cells than for inner hair cells.
source: Remarkably, the stiffness gradient was steeper (*p<0.05; Figure 2—source data 1) for outer hair cells than for inner hair cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the experimental data with p-value provided.

claim: At each cochlear position, outer hair-cell bundles were stiffer than inner hair-cell bundles.
source: At each cochlear position, outer hair-cell bundles were stiffer than inner hair-cell bundles, with a stiffness ratio that increased from the apex to the base of the organ.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The stiffness ratio between outer and inner hair-cell bundles increased from the apex to the base of the organ.
source: At each cochlear position, outer hair-cell bundles were stiffer than inner hair-cell bundles, with a stiffness ratio that increased from the apex to the base of the organ.
evidence: This is derived from the comparative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Force-displacement relations measured with fluid-jet stimulation were remarkably linear, showing no sign of gating compliance.
source: As also observed by others using fluid-jet stimulation of cochlear hair cells (Géléoc et al., 1997; Corns et al., 2014), we measured force-displacement relations that were remarkably linear (Figure 2B and D), showing no sign of gating compliance (Howard and Hudspeth, 1988).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with citations to similar findings.

claim: The rise time of fluid-jet stimuli may have been too long to outspeed fast adaptation, masking gating compliance.
source: First, the rise time (~500 µs; Figure 2—figure supplement 3) of our fluid-jet stimuli may have been too long to outspeed fast adaptation, masking gating compliance (Kennedy et al., 2003; Tinevez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a possible explanation for the linear force-displacement relations, supported by citations.

claim: Gating forces may have been too weak to affect hair-bundle mechanics under the experimental conditions.
source: Second, gating forces – the change in tip-link tension evoked by gating of the transduction channels (Markin and Hudspeth, 1995) − may have been too weak to affect hair-bundle mechanics under our experimental conditions (Fettiplace, 2006; Beurg et al., 2008).
evidence: This is another possible explanation for the linear force-displacement relations, supported by citations.

claim: Between the 1-kHz and the 4-kHz positions, the gating-spring stiffness increased by 520% for outer hair cells.
source: Between the 1-kHz and the 4-kHz positions, the gating-spring stiffness increased by 520% for outer hair cells but only by 300% for inner hair cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from the experimental data.

claim: Between the 1-kHz and the 4-kHz positions, the gating-spring stiffness increased by 300% for inner hair cells.
source: Between the 1-kHz and the 4-kHz positions, the gating-spring stiffness increased by 520% for outer hair cells but only by 300% for inner hair cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from the experimental data.

claim: With inner hair cells, there was no significant variation of the rotational stiffness between the 1- and 2-kHz locations as well as between the 4- and 15-kHz locations.
source: Similarly, with inner hair cells, there was no significant variation of the rotational stiffness between the 1- and 2-kHz locations as well as between the 4- and 15-kHz locations, although we observed an increase by 100% between the 2- and 4-kHz locations (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was an increase by 100% in rotational stiffness of inner hair cells between the 2- and 4-kHz locations.
source: Similarly, with inner hair cells, there was no significant variation of the rotational stiffness between the 1- and 2-kHz locations as well as between the 4- and 15-kHz locations, although we observed an increase by 100% between the 2- and 4-kHz locations (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The hair-bundle morphology is not the sole determinant of hair-bundle mechanics.
source: The hair-bundle morphology is not the sole determinant of hair-bundle mechanics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that morphology cannot explain all observed gradients.

claim: The transduction channels close when the tip links are disrupted.
source: The transduction channels close when the tip links are disrupted, indicating that the channels are inherently more stable in a closed state (Assad et al., 1991; Beurg et al., 2008; Indzhykulian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The transduction channels are inherently more stable in a closed state.
source: The transduction channels close when the tip links are disrupted, indicating that the channels are inherently more stable in a closed state (Assad et al., 1991; Beurg et al., 2008; Indzhykulian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that channels close upon tip-link disruption, supported by citations.

claim: Tip-link tension brings the operating point of the transducer within the steep region of the sigmoidal relation between the channels' open probability and the position of the hair bundle.
source: In functional hair bundles, tip-link tension is thought to bring the operating point of the transducer within the steep region of the sigmoidal relation between the channels' open probability and the position of the hair bundle, ensuring sensitive detection of hair-bundle deflections.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of tip-link tension based on established models.

claim: If there is tension in the tip links, then disrupting these links must result in a positive offset in the resting position of the hair bundle.
source: If there is tension in the tip links, then disrupting these links must result in a positive offset in the resting position of the hair bundle (Assad et al., 1991; Jaramillo and Hudspeth, 1993).
evidence: This is a logical prediction supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The positive movement of the hair bundle upon EDTA iontophoresis was associated with a decrease in hair-bundle stiffness and closure of the transduction channels.
source: Consistent with tip-link disruption, this movement was associated with a decrease in hair-bundle stiffness, as well as with closure of the transduction channels and loss of transduction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The positive offset in resting position upon tip-link disruption was observed at all positions explored along the tonotopic axis of the cochlea, both for inner and outer hair cells.
source: The positive offset in resting position upon tip-link disruption was observed at all positions that we explored along the tonotopic axis of the cochlea, both for inner and outer hair cells, demonstrating that the hair bundles were indeed under tension (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The magnitude of the positive movement upon tip-link disruption increased significantly from 9 ± 3 nm (n = 13) to 45 ± 10 nm (n = 12) for outer hair cells with characteristic frequencies that increased from 1 to 4 kHz.
source: In addition, we observed that the magnitude of the evoked movement increased significantly (**p<0.01; Figure 5—source data 1) from 9 ± 3 nm (n = 13) to 45 ± 10 nm (n = 12) for outer hair cells with characteristic frequencies that increased from 1 to 4 kHz.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical significance indicated.

claim: There was no significant difference in the positive offset among inner hair cells with characteristic frequencies that varied within the 1–15-kHz range.
source: In contrast, we observed no significant difference among inner hair cells with characteristic frequencies that varied within the 1–15-kHz range (p>0.05; Figure 5—source data 1): the positive offset was 21 ± 2 nm (n = 71) over the whole ensemble of inner hair cells.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The positive offset was 21 ± 2 nm (n = 71) over the whole ensemble of inner hair cells.
source: In contrast, we observed no significant difference among inner hair cells with characteristic frequencies that varied within the 1–15-kHz range (p>0.05; Figure 5—source data 1): the positive offset was 21 ± 2 nm (n = 71) over the whole ensemble of inner hair cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Within the range of cochlear locations explored, there was a steep gradient of hair-bundle tension for outer hair cells but a comparatively weaker gradient for inner hair cells.
source: As a result, within the range of cochlear locations that we explored, we measured a steep gradient of hair-bundle tension for outer hair cells but a comparatively weaker gradient (*p<0.05; Figure 5—source data 1) for inner hair cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The hair-bundle tension increased by nearly 13-fold from 18 ± 7 pN (n = 15) to 248 ± 59 pN (n = 17) for outer hair cells with characteristic frequencies from 1 to 4 kHz.
source: The hair-bundle tension increased by nearly 13-fold from 18 ± 7 pN (n = 15) to 248 ± 59 pN (n = 17) for outer hair cells (characteristic frequencies: 1−4 kHz) but by only 3.3-fold from 24 ± 5 pN (n = 33) to 100 ± 22 pN (n = 12) for inner hair cells (characteristic frequencies: 1−15 kHz).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The hair-bundle tension increased by 3.3-fold from 24 ± 5 pN (n = 33) to 100 ± 22 pN (n = 12) for inner hair cells with characteristic frequencies from 1 to 15 kHz.
source: The hair-bundle tension increased by nearly 13-fold from 18 ± 7 pN (n = 15) to 248 ± 59 pN (n = 17) for outer hair cells (characteristic frequencies: 1−4 kHz) but by only 3.3-fold from 24 ± 5 pN (n = 33) to 100 ± 22 pN (n = 12) for inner hair cells (characteristic frequencies: 1−15 kHz).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Tension in a single tip link showed gradients along the tonotopic axis.
source: Remarkably, the observed gradients in hair-bundle tension (Figure 5B) were not only due to an increase in the number of tip links that contributed to this tension (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), for tension in a single tip link also showed gradients (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The single tip-link tension was comparable in the two types of cells at the 1-kHz location: 4.7 ± 2.0 pN (n = 23) for outer hair cells and 5.9 ± 1.3 pN (n = 43) for inner hair cells.
source: The single tip-link tension was comparable in the two types of cells at the 1-kHz location: 4.7 ± 2.0 pN (n = 23) for outer hair cells and 5.9 ± 1.3 pN (n = 43) for inner hair cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: At the 4-kHz location, the single tip-link tension had increased by 620% to 34 ± 8 pN (n = 19) in outer hair cells.
source: However, at the 4-kHz location, the single tip-link tension had increased by 620% to 34 ± 8 pN (n = 19) in outer hair cells but only by 170% to 16 ± 4 pN (n = 17) in inner hair cells; at the 15-kHz location, tip-link tension in inner hair cells was 19 ± 5 pN (n = 18).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: At the 4-kHz location, the single tip-link tension had increased by 170% to 16 ± 4 pN (n = 17) in inner hair cells.
source: However, at the 4-kHz location, the single tip-link tension had increased by 620% to 34 ± 8 pN (n = 19) in outer hair cells but only by 170% to 16 ± 4 pN (n = 17) in inner hair cells; at the 15-kHz location, tip-link tension in inner hair cells was 19 ± 5 pN (n = 18).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: At the 15-kHz location, tip-link tension in inner hair cells was 19 ± 5 pN (n = 18).
source: However, at the 4-kHz location, the single tip-link tension had increased by 620% to 34 ± 8 pN (n = 19) in outer hair cells but only by 170% to 16 ± 4 pN (n = 17) in inner hair cells; at the 15-kHz location, tip-link tension in inner hair cells was 19 ± 5 pN (n = 18).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: A linear regression confirmed that the gradient of single tip-link tension was significantly steeper for outer hair cells than for inner hair cells.
source: A linear regression of the relation between the single tip-link tension and the characteristic frequency confirmed that the gradient was significantly (*p<0.05; Figure 5—source data 1) steeper for outer hair cells.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The hair bundle first moved in the negative direction in response to an iontophoretic step of EDTA, before the directionality of the movement reverted and the bundle showed the positive movement associated with tip-link disruption.
source: The dynamic response to an iontophoretic step of EDTA, and thus to a decrease of the extracellular Ca2+ concentration, was biphasic. The hair bundle first moved in the negative direction (arrowhead in Figure 4A), before the directionality of the movement reverted and the bundle showed the positive movement associated with tip-link disruption.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The negative movement was associated with an increased inward current of similar time course.
source: The negative movement was associated with an increased inward current of similar time course (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The evoked decrease in the extracellular Ca2+ concentration resulted in an increase in gating-spring tension, which both pulled the hair bundle in the negative direction and led to the opening of the transduction channels.
source: Within the framework of the gating-spring model of mechanoelectrical transduction (Corey and Hudspeth, 1983; Markin and Hudspeth, 1995), this observation is readily explained if the evoked decrease in the extracellular Ca2+ concentration resulted in an increase in gating-spring tension, which both pulled the hair bundle in the negative direction and led to the opening of the transduction channels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations within an established theoretical framework.

claim: Going from the 1-kHz location to the 4-kHz location, the maximal tip-link tension displayed a gradient from 14 ± 4 pN (n = 30) to 54 ± 12 pN (n = 23) in outer hair cells.
source: Going from the 1-kHz location to the 4-kHz location, this maximal tip-link tension displayed a gradient from 14 ± 4 pN (n = 30) to 54 ± 12 pN (n = 23) in outer hair cells and from 15 ± 3 pN (n = 49) to 44 ± 8 pN (n = 39) in inner hair cells; the maximal tension in inner hair cells at the 15-kHz location was not significantly different than at the 4-kHz location.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Going from the 1-kHz location to the 4-kHz location, the maximal tip-link tension displayed a gradient from 15 ± 3 pN (n = 49) to 44 ± 8 pN (n = 39) in inner hair cells.
source: Going from the 1-kHz location to the 4-kHz location, this maximal tip-link tension displayed a gradient from 14 ± 4 pN (n = 30) to 54 ± 12 pN (n = 23) in outer hair cells and from 15 ± 3 pN (n = 49) to 44 ± 8 pN (n = 39) in inner hair cells; the maximal tension in inner hair cells at the 15-kHz location was not significantly different than at the 4-kHz location.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The maximal tension in inner hair cells at the 15-kHz location was not significantly different than at the 4-kHz location.
source: Going from the 1-kHz location to the 4-kHz location, this maximal tip-link tension displayed a gradient from 14 ± 4 pN (n = 30) to 54 ± 12 pN (n = 23) in outer hair cells and from 15 ± 3 pN (n = 49) to 44 ± 8 pN (n = 39) in inner hair cells; the maximal tension in inner hair cells at the 15-kHz location was not significantly different than at the 4-kHz location.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: When immersing the hair cells in saline with 500 µM Ca2+, the negative movements could be reversible.
source: However, in six different preparations for which the hair bundle was immersed in saline with a higher Ca2+ concentration (500 µM) than usual (20 µM), we were able to preserve the integrity of the tip links and demonstrate that the negative movements could be reversible (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The absolute magnitude and the speed of the negative movement increased with the magnitude of the iontophoretic current.
source: Under such conditions, we observed that the absolute magnitude and the speed of the negative movement increased with the magnitude of the iontophoretic current.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the reversible negative movement experiments.

claim: The hair bundle reached a new steady-state position when the iontophoretic step was long enough.
source: Notably, the hair bundle reached a new steady-state position when the iontophoretic step was long enough (Figure 6E), suggesting that resting tension in the tip links could be modulated by the extracellular Ca2+ concentration, with higher tensions at lower Ca2+ concentrations.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Resting tension in the tip links could be modulated by the extracellular Ca2+ concentration, with higher tensions at lower Ca2+ concentrations.
source: Notably, the hair bundle reached a new steady-state position when the iontophoretic step was long enough (Figure 6E), suggesting that resting tension in the tip links could be modulated by the extracellular Ca2+ concentration, with higher tensions at lower Ca2+ concentrations.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Tonotopy of the mammalian cochlea is known to be associated with gradients of hair-bundle morphology.
source: Tonotopy of the mammalian cochlea is known to be associated with gradients of hair-bundle morphology (Wright, 1984; Lim, 1986; Roth and Bruns, 1992; Tilney et al., 1992), as well as of electrophysiological properties of the transduction apparatus (Ricci et al., 2003; Ricci et al., 2005; Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Beurg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Tonotopy of the mammalian cochlea is known to be associated with gradients of electrophysiological properties of the transduction apparatus.
source: Tonotopy of the mammalian cochlea is known to be associated with gradients of hair-bundle morphology (Wright, 1984; Lim, 1986; Roth and Bruns, 1992; Tilney et al., 1992), as well as of electrophysiological properties of the transduction apparatus (Ricci et al., 2003; Ricci et al., 2005; Fettiplace and Kim, 2014; Beurg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The gating springs that control the open probability of the mechanoelectrical transduction channels are stiffer in hair cells that respond to higher characteristic frequencies.
source: Specifically, by dissecting the relative contributions of the tip links and of the stereociliary pivots to the micromechanical properties of the hair bundle, we found that the gating springs that control the open probability of the mechanoelectrical transduction channels are stiffer (Figure 3D) and subjected to higher mechanical tension (Figure 5C) in hair cells that respond to higher characteristic frequencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The gating springs are subjected to higher mechanical tension in hair cells that respond to higher characteristic frequencies.
source: Specifically, by dissecting the relative contributions of the tip links and of the stereociliary pivots to the micromechanical properties of the hair bundle, we found that the gating springs that control the open probability of the mechanoelectrical transduction channels are stiffer (Figure 3D) and subjected to higher mechanical tension (Figure 5C) in hair cells that respond to higher characteristic frequencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The data raises the possibility of a mechanical role of the tip-link complex in the process that sets the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
source: In return, our data raises the possibility of a mechanical role of the tip-link complex in the process that sets the characteristic frequency of the hair cell, at least within the apical cochlear region that we probed in this study.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The measured stiffness ratios were ~50% and ~70% larger than those expected from morphology for outer and inner hair cells, respectively.
source: Computing the stiffness ratio between the most basal and the most apical cochlear location that we were able to probe, the measured stiffness ratios (Figure 2E) were ~50% and ~70% larger than those expected from morphology for outer and inner hair cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between measured and predicted stiffness ratios.

claim: Intrinsic gradients of the single gating-spring stiffness are the consequence of the steeper stiffness gradients than expected from morphology.
source: We interpret this result as the consequence of intrinsic gradients of the single gating-spring stiffness (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between measured and predicted stiffness gradients.

claim: Stiffness gradients of hair bundles with disrupted tip links are entirely determined by morphology.
source: Stiffness gradients of hair bundles with disrupted tip links are thus entirely determined by morphology, in contradistinction to those observed with intact hair bundles.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the finding that pivot stiffness gradients match morphological predictions.

claim: Experiments were performed with hair cells from juvenile animals (P7-P10), before the onset of hearing.
source: Our experiments were performed with hair cells from juvenile animals (P7-P10), before the onset of hearing.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Hair-cell maturation progresses from base to apex in the cochlea.
source: Hair-cell maturation progresses from base to apex in the cochlea (Wu and Kelley, 2012), which may thus have affected our estimates of mechanical gradients of the tip-link complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: 92% of recordings were performed at P8 or later.
source: However, because 92% of our recordings were performed at P8 or later (Materials and methods), the tip-link complex ought to be nearly mature in our experiments, at least in outer hair cells (Roth and Bruns, 1992; Waguespack et al., 2007; Beurg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: The tip-link complex ought to be nearly mature at P8 or later, at least in outer hair cells.
source: However, because 92% of our recordings were performed at P8 or later (Materials and methods), the tip-link complex ought to be nearly mature in our experiments, at least in outer hair cells (Roth and Bruns, 1992; Waguespack et al., 2007; Beurg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental timeline supported by citations.

claim: The hair-bundle stiffness increased by 240% over two octaves (1‒4 kHz) of characteristic frequencies for outer hair cells.
source: We observed that the hair-bundle stiffness increased by 240% over two octaves (1‒4 kHz) of characteristic frequencies for outer hair cells and by a similar amount but over 4 octaves (1‒15 kHz) for inner hair cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The hair-bundle stiffness increased by a similar amount over 4 octaves (1‒15 kHz) for inner hair cells.
source: We observed that the hair-bundle stiffness increased by 240% over two octaves (1‒4 kHz) of characteristic frequencies for outer hair cells and by a similar amount but over 4 octaves (1‒15 kHz) for inner hair cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: If the stiffness gradient continued along the same trend toward more basal locations, the base-to-apex stiffness ratio would be ~40 for outer hair cells.
source: If it were the case, we would expect a base-to-apex stiffness ratio of ~40 for outer hair cells, which is comparable to the base-to-apex ratio of characteristic frequencies in the rat cochlea (range: 0.5–50 kHz; Viberg and Canlon, 2004), but only of ~6 for inner hair cells.
evidence: This is a hypothetical extrapolation from the measured data.

claim: If the stiffness gradient continued along the same trend toward more basal locations, the base-to-apex stiffness ratio would be ~6 for inner hair cells.
source: If it were the case, we would expect a base-to-apex stiffness ratio of ~40 for outer hair cells, which is comparable to the base-to-apex ratio of characteristic frequencies in the rat cochlea (range: 0.5–50 kHz; Viberg and Canlon, 2004), but only of ~6 for inner hair cells.
evidence: This is a hypothetical extrapolation from the measured data.

claim: The base-to-apex ratio of characteristic frequencies in the rat cochlea ranges from 0.5 to 50 kHz.
source: If it were the case, we would expect a base-to-apex stiffness ratio of ~40 for outer hair cells, which is comparable to the base-to-apex ratio of characteristic frequencies in the rat cochlea (range: 0.5–50 kHz; Viberg and Canlon, 2004), but only of ~6 for inner hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Two orders of magnitude in frequency must be produced by a 10,000-fold increase in stiffness for a passive spring-mass resonance mechanism.
source: Assuming for simplicity that the bundle's mass remains nearly the same along the tonotopic axis (Tilney and Tilney, 1988), two orders of magnitude in frequency must be produced by a 10,000-fold increase in stiffness, corresponding to much steeper gradients than those reported here.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the physics of spring-mass systems.

claim: The hair bundle could actively resonate with sound as the result of spontaneous oscillations.
source: Alternatively, it has been proposed that the hair bundle could actively resonate with sound as the result of spontaneous oscillations (Martin et al., 2001; Hudspeth, 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The characteristic frequency is set by the frequency of the oscillator, which is expected to increase with the stiffness of the hair bundle.
source: Within this framework, the characteristic frequency is set by the frequency of the oscillator, which is expected to increase with the stiffness of the hair bundle (Vilfan and Duke, 2003; Tinevez et al., 2007; Martin, 2008; Barral et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: The relation between oscillator frequency and stiffness may be steeper than that resulting from a passive spring-mass system, possibly approximating a linear dependence.
source: Notably, the relation may be steeper than that resulting from a passive spring-mass system, possibly approximating a linear dependence (Hudspeth et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by a citation.

claim: The stiffness gradient observed for outer hair cells could be steep enough to be a major determinant of the tonotopic map in an active resonance framework.
source: In this case, the stiffness gradient observed here (Figure 2E) for outer hair cells, but not for inner hair cells, could be steep enough to be a major determinant of the tonotopic map.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the measured gradients to theoretical predictions.

claim: A gradient of tip-link tension ought to result in a gradient of open probability of the transduction channels.
source: Tip-link tension is thought to control the open probability of the transduction channels, with higher tension promoting opening of the channels (Hudspeth and Gillespie, 1994). On this basis, a gradient of tip-link tension (Figure 5C) ought to result in a gradient of open probability.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the established relationship between tension and open probability.

claim: The channels' open probability remains remarkably uniform along the tonotopic axis in outer hair cells, near a value of ½.
source: Yet, it has been shown in outer hair cells that the channels' open probability—the operating point of the transducer—remains remarkably uniform along the tonotopic axis, near a value of ½ (Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The tension gradient for outer hair cells is associated with a gradient of single-channel conductance.
source: To explain this observation, we note that the tension gradient for outer hair cells is associated with a gradient of single-channel conductance (Beurg et al., 2006; Beurg et al., 2015; Beurg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The magnitude of the Ca2+ influx into transducing stereocilia is expected to increase with the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
source: As a consequence, the magnitude of the Ca2+ influx into transducing stereocilia is expected to increase with the characteristic frequency of the hair cell.
evidence: This is an inference from the gradient of single-channel conductance.

claim: The transduction channels close at increased Ca2+ concentrations.
source: Manipulations that affect the extracellular or the intracellular Ca2+ concentration indicate that the transduction channels close at increased Ca2+ concentrations (reviewed in Fettiplace and Kim, 2014), possibly because the channels are harder to open when the Ca2+ concentration is higher near the channel's pore (Cheung and Corey, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review and primary literature.

claim: The gradient of tip-link tension may compensate for the effects of the conductance gradient on the open probability.
source: Thus, the gradient of tip-link tension reported here (Figure 5C) may compensate for the effects of the conductance gradient on the open probability: channels with higher conductance impart higher Ca2+ influxes (closing the channels) but are also subjected to higher tension (opening the channels), perhaps maintaining an optimal operating point for the transducer at all cochlear locations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the uniform open probability despite tension gradients.

claim: Tension in the tip links is thought to be produced actively by pulling forces from molecular motors interacting with the actin core of the stereocilia at the upper insertion point of the tip link.
source: Tension in the tip links is thought to be produced actively by pulling forces from molecular motors interacting with the actin core of the stereocilia at the upper insertion point of the tip link (Gillespie and Müller, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The observed tension gradient implies that, towards basal cochlear locations, there are more motors or that each motor exerts higher forces than near the apex.
source: The observed tension gradient in turn implies that, towards basal cochlear locations, there are more motors or that each motor exerts higher forces than near the apex.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed tension gradient.

claim: The tip links of inner-hair-cell bundles were found to bear less tension than those of outer-hair-cell bundles.
source: Notably, the tip links of inner-hair-cell bundles were found to bear less tension than those of outer-hair-cell bundles (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental data shown in Figures 5B-C.

claim: The open probability of the transduction channels is thought to be smaller in inner hair cells than in outer hair cells.
source: This property qualitatively makes sense, for the open probability of the transduction channels is thought to be smaller in inner hair cells than in outer hair cells (Russell and Sellick, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: There is no, or only a weak, gradient of the single-channel conductance in inner hair cells.
source: There is also no, or only a weak, gradient of the single-channel conductance in inner hair cells (Beurg et al., 2006; Beurg et al., 2018), which parallels the relatively weak gradient of tip-link tension observed here.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The tip link is composed of the association of two cadherin-related proteins, cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15 (PCDH15).
source: The tip link is composed of the association of two cadherin-related proteins, cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15 (PCDH15) (Kazmierczak et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations have suggested that a bend between extracellular cadherin (EC) repeats 9 and 10 of PCDH15 may confer some compliance to otherwise rigid tip links.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations have suggested that a bend between extracellular cadherin (EC) repeats 9 and 10 of PCDH15 may confer some compliance to otherwise rigid tip links (Araya-Secchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a molecular dynamics study.

claim: Tensions higher than ~10 pN are predicted to evoke complete unbending of EC9-10, resulting in significant stiffening of the tip link.
source: Tensions higher than ~10 pN are predicted to evoke complete unbending of EC9-10, resulting in significant stiffening of the tip link.
evidence: This is a prediction from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The estimates of tip-link tension are compatible with a contribution of the bending elasticity of EC9-10 to gating-spring stiffness at the apex of the rat cochlea, especially in inner hair cells.
source: Assuming that PCDH15 in the tip link forms a dimer (Kazmierczak et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2018) and that tip-link tension is equally shared by the two filaments, our estimates of tip-link tension (Figure 5C) are compatible with a contribution of the bending elasticity of EC9-10 to gating-spring stiffness at the apex of the rat cochlea, especially in inner hair cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measured tension values in the context of molecular structure.

claim: In outer hair cells, tension may quickly become too high to allow a bent conformation in EC9-10 as one progresses from the very apex towards more basal cochlear locations.
source: In outer hair cells, as one progresses from the very apex towards more basal cochlear locations, tension may quickly become too high to allow a bent conformation in EC9-10.
evidence: This is an inference from the measured tension values.

claim: At the 4 kHz location, the resting tip-link tension was estimated at ~35 pN.
source: At the 4 kHz location, we estimated a resting tip-link tension of ~35 pN.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Tip-link tension might be high enough to evoke unfolding of EC domains, at least under resting conditions or at physiological loading rates.
source: Taking the measured unfolding forces of Ig domains in titin as a reference (Rief et al., 1997), tip-link tension might actually be high enough to evoke unfolding of EC domains, at least under resting conditions or at physiological loading rates.
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison to unfolding forces in other proteins.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that unfolding a various number of EC domains may contribute to a gradation of gating-spring stiffness.
source: Recent evidence suggests that unfolding a various number of EC domains may contribute to a gradation of gating-spring stiffness (Bartsch et al., 2018; Bartsch and Hudspeth, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: The estimated gradients of gating-spring tension were associated with gradients of gating-spring stiffness: stiffer gating springs are subjected to more resting tension.
source: Notably, the estimated gradients of gating-spring tension (Figure 5C) were associated with gradients of gating-spring stiffness (Figure 3D): stiffer gating springs are subjected to more resting tension.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the data in Figures 3D and 5C.

claim: Strain stiffening is a common phenomenon associated with the entropic elasticity of macromolecules, including the tip-link component PCDH15.
source: Strain stiffening is a common phenomenon associated with the entropic elasticity of macromolecules, including the tip-link component PCDH15 (Bartsch et al., 2018), as well as with filamentous protein networks (Bustamante et al., 1994; Rief et al., 1997; Kang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on protein mechanics.

claim: A tension gradient may in part explain the existence of the observed gradient of gating-spring stiffness.
source: A tension gradient may thus in part explain the existence of the observed gradient of gating-spring stiffness.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the phenomenon of strain stiffening.

claim: The gating-spring stiffness could vary if the gating spring were composed of a variable number of compliant molecules operating in parallel and connected to a single tip link.
source: Alternatively, the gating-spring stiffness could vary if the gating spring were composed of a variable number of compliant molecules operating in parallel and connected to a single tip link.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis for the observed stiffness gradient.

claim: Upon iontophoretic application of EDTA, before tip-link disruption, the hair bundle first moved in the negative direction and this movement was associated with a concomitant opening of the transduction channels.
source: Upon iontophoretic application of a Ca2+ chelator (EDTA), before tip-link disruption, we observed that the hair bundle first moved in the negative direction and that this movement was associated with a concomitant opening of the transduction channels (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lowering the extracellular Ca2+ concentration is expected to increase the magnitude of the current flowing through open transduction channels but not to produce hair-bundle movements as the result of block release only.
source: Calcium acts as a permeant channel blocker of the transduction channels (Fettiplace and Kim, 2014). Lowering the extracellular Ca2+ concentration is thus expected to increase the magnitude of the current flowing through open transduction channels but not to produce hair-bundle movements, at least as the result of block release only.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of Ca2+ as a channel blocker.

claim: A decrease of the extracellular Ca2+ concentration promotes opening of the transduction channels.
source: A decrease of the extracellular Ca2+ concentration also promotes opening of the transduction channels (Hacohen et al., 1989; Johnson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Within the framework of the gating-spring model, channel opening must reduce gating-spring extension and in turn tension, fostering positive movements of the hair bundle.
source: Within the framework of the gating-spring model of mechanoelectrical transduction, channel opening must reduce gating-spring extension and in turn tension, fostering positive movements of the hair bundle.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the gating-spring model.

claim: The observed negative movements are readily explained if the evoked reduction of extracellular Ca2+ concentration resulted in an increase of tip-link tension.
source: Instead, our observations are readily explained if the evoked reduction of extracellular Ca2+ concentration resulted in an increase of tip-link (and thus gating-spring) tension.
evidence: This is the interpretation proposed to explain the negative movements.

claim: If tip-link tension at rest is set by myosin molecular motors that pull on the tip links, then the motor force must increase at decreased Ca2+ concentrations.
source: If tip-link tension at rest is set by myosin molecular motors that pull on the tip links (Hudspeth and Gillespie, 1994), then the motor force must increase at decreased Ca2+ concentrations.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the interpretation that Ca2+ reduction increases tip-link tension.

claim: A negative deflection would be produced if lowering the extracellular Ca2+ concentration evoked stiffening or shortening of the gating springs, increasing tension in the tip links.
source: Alternatively, a negative deflection would also be produced if lowering the extracellular Ca2+ concentration evoked stiffening (Martin et al., 2003; Beurg et al., 2008) or shortening of the gating springs, increasing tension in the tip links.
evidence: This is an alternative explanation supported by citations.

claim: A Ca2+-dependent regulation of tip-link tension via a change of gating-spring stiffness or length appears unlikely because slow adaptation was observed.
source: Because we observed the mechanical correlate of slow adaptation in response to force steps (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), a Ca2+-dependent regulation of tip-link tension via a change of gating-spring stiffness or length appears unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of slow adaptation.

claim: Calcium ions have been proposed to interact extracellularly with the local lipid environment of the transduction channels, promoting lower values of the channels' open probability.
source: Calcium ions have indeed been proposed to interact extracellularly with the local lipid environment of the transduction channels, promoting lower values of the channels' open probability (Peng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: The recordings are consistent with the hypothesis that Ca2+ interacts with the local lipid environment of the transduction channels.
source: Our recordings (Figure 4B and Figure 6D–E) are consistent with this hypothesis but a change in membrane mechanics would not explain the observed steady-state increase in tip-link tension (Figure 6E) if slow adaptation happens in these cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data in the context of a proposed mechanism.

claim: Depolarization of rat outer hair cells was previously shown to evoke positive movements of the hair bundle.
source: Interestingly, depolarization of rat outer hair cells was previously shown to evoke positive movements of the hair bundle (Kennedy et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Both depolarization and chelation of extracellular Ca2+ are expected to reduce the intracellular Ca2+ concentration in the vicinity of the transduction channel's pore.
source: Both depolarization and chelation of extracellular Ca2+ are expected to reduce the intracellular Ca2+ concentration in the vicinity of the transduction channel's pore.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known effects of these manipulations.

claim: The directionality of active hair-bundle movements is opposite between depolarization and Ca2+ chelation studies, suggesting that the hair bundle can operate in two regimes.
source: Yet, the directionality of active hair-bundle movements is opposite in the two studies, suggesting that the hair bundle can operate in two regimes (Tinevez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the contrasting results supported by a citation.

claim: In the first regime, the response to Ca2+ changes is dominated by gating forces so that the resting tension in the tip links is nearly the same before and after application of the stimulus.
source: In the first regime (Kennedy et al., 2006), the response to Ca2+ changes is dominated by gating forces (Howard and Hudspeth, 1988) so that the resting tension in the tip links is nearly the same before and after application of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of one operating regime supported by citations.

claim: In the other regime, Ca2+-evoked changes of the resting tension in the tip links dominate gating forces.
source: In the other regime (our study), Ca2+-evoked changes of the resting tension in the tip links (Figure 6) dominate gating forces.
evidence: This is a description of the operating regime observed in this study.

claim: In the chicken cochlea, depolarization of the hair cell was reported to evoke negative movements of the hair bundle.
source: In the chicken cochlea, depolarization of the hair cell was reported to evoke negative movements of the hair bundle (Beurg et al., 2013), a directionality in agreement with that found here (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work in chicken cochlea.

claim: The response of different hair cells to a given Ca2+ change can be of either directionality.
source: In addition, it has been shown in the bullfrog's sacculus (Tinevez et al., 2007) and the turtle's cochlea (Ricci et al., 2002) that the response of different hair cells to a given Ca2+ change can be of either directionality and that the directionality of the response for a given hair cell can even be reversed by applying a position offset to the hair bundle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to work in other species.

claim: The two regimes of active hair-bundle motility can potentially coexist within the same hair cell, but only if gating forces are strong enough.
source: The two regimes of active hair-bundle motility can thus potentially coexist within the same hair cell, but only if gating forces are strong enough (Tinevez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by a citation.

claim: Gating forces were relatively weak under the experimental conditions of this study.
source: This observation confirms that gating forces were relatively weak under our experimental conditions, although others have shown that gating compliance can be measured with mammalian cochlear hair cells (Russell et al., 1992; Kennedy et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference from the linear force-displacement relations observed.

claim: Stiffness and tension gradients were steeper for outer hair cells than for inner hair cells.
source: Stiffness (Figure 2E) and tension (Figure 5B) gradients were steeper for outer hair cells, which serve primarily as mechanical amplifiers of sound-evoked vibrations, than for inner hair cells, the true sensors of the inner ear (Hudspeth, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative data shown in Figures 2E and 5B.

claim: The division of labor between inner and outer hair cells may impart more stringent regulatory constrains to outer hair cells to tune their mechanoreceptive antenna according to the local characteristic frequency of the cochlear partition.
source: Thus, the division of labor between inner and outer hair cells may impart more stringent regulatory constrains to outer hair cells to tune their mechanoreceptive antenna according to the local characteristic frequency of the cochlear partition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the steeper gradients observed in outer hair cells.

claim: The exact contribution of the hair bundle to frequency tuning remains unsure.
source: However, the exact contribution of the hair bundle to frequency tuning remains unsure and, more generally, the mechanism that specifies the characteristic frequency remains a fundamental problem in auditory physiology.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Frequency selectivity cannot be ascribed to one element only.
source: This may be in part because frequency selectivity cannot be ascribed to one element only, for instance the passive resonant property of the basilar membrane that was characterized in the pioneering work of von Békésy (Von Békésy and Wever, 1960).
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of cochlear mechanics supported by a citation.

claim: The characteristic frequency emerges from an active dynamic interplay between somatic electromotility of outer hair cells and the micromechanical environment.
source: Various models of cochlear mechanics instead indicate that the characteristic frequency emerges from an active dynamic interplay between somatic electromotility of outer hair cells (Ashmore, 2008) and the micromechanical environment, including the basilar and tectorial membranes, as well as the hair bundle (Nobili and Mammano, 1996; Hudspeth et al., 2010; O Maoiléidigh and Jülicher, 2010; Meaud and Grosh, 2011; Hudspeth, 2014; Reichenbach and Hudspeth, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple modeling studies.

claim: Mechanical tuning of the inner constituents of the cochlear partition appears to happen at many scales: from the mesoscopic scale of the basilar and tectorial membranes, to the cellular scale of the hair bundle and hair-cell soma, down to the molecular scale of the hair cell's transduction apparatus.
source: Mechanical tuning of the inner constituents of the cochlear partition appears to happen at many scales: from the mesoscopic scale of the basilar and tectorial membranes, to the cellular scale of the hair bundle and hair-cell soma, down to the molecular scale of the hair cell's transduction apparatus.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the multi-scale nature of cochlear tuning.

claim: Tonotopy is associated with stiffness and tension gradients of the tip-link complex, in addition to other factors.
source: Our work demonstrates that tonotopy is associated, in addition to other factors, with stiffness and tension gradients of the tip-link complex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics committee on animal experimentation of the Institut Curie.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics committee on animal experimentation of the Institut Curie; they complied with the European and French National Regulation for the Protection of Vertebrate Animals used for Experimental and other Scientific Purposes (Directive 2010/63; French Decree 2013–118).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Experiments were performed on excised cochlear coils of Sprague Dawley rats between postnatal day 7 and 10 (P7–P10).
source: Experiments were performed on excised cochlear coils of Sprague Dawley rats (Janvier Labs) between postnatal day 7 and 10 (P7–P10), with 8% of the cells at P7, 75% at P8‒P9 and 17% at P10.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and timing.

claim: 8% of the cells were at P7, 75% at P8‒P9 and 17% at P10.
source: Experiments were performed on excised cochlear coils of Sprague Dawley rats (Janvier Labs) between postnatal day 7 and 10 (P7–P10), with 8% of the cells at P7, 75% at P8‒P9 and 17% at P10.
evidence: This describes the distribution of developmental ages in the sample.

claim: The horizontal projected distance between the mouth of the fluid-jet pipette and the hair bundle was set at ~8 µm.
source: The horizontal projected distance between the mouth of the pipette (blue vertical line) and the hair bundle (green vertical line) was set at ~8 µm.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1C.
